Lailashi New Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Lailashi, Georgia

Not demolished. Lailashi was once the largest Jewish settlement in western Georgia, with Jews arriving in the 17th century following Ottoman persecution in Akhaltsikhe; some believe the village's name derives from the Hebrew 'laila' (night). By the early 20th century, 1,200 Jews made up most of the village's population, trading alongside Armenians and Greeks along a historic caravan route. Two synagogues served the community, the second built in 1910; both closed under Soviet religious suppression in 1923-24. The community steadily shrank through the 20th century - 235 Jews in 1939, just 20 by 1970, none today. Lailashi's abandoned synagogue once housed the extraordinary 'Lailashi Codex,' a 10th-11th century handwritten Torah manuscript believed by legend to have arrived floating down a river, now preserved at Georgia's National Manuscript Center alongside the Bible of Breti. This 'New' cemetery, one of two in the village, holds tombstones from 1865 onward; active use ended in 1974, though a few Kutaisi Jews were buried here in the 1980s.
